newsitem.title: USA: Simpson fends off barrage of accusations.
newsitem.headline: Simpson fends off barrage of accusations.

text.p: O.J. Simpson ended his second grueling day on the witness stand in his civil trial on Monday, fending off a barrage of accusations that he murdered his ex-wife and her friend and admitting he had contemplated suicide.

Daniel Petrocelli, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs in the case, contended Simpson was planning to kill himself during the infamous Bronco freeway chase on June 17, 1994, "because you knew you were going to spend the rest of your life in jail."
"No, that's incorrect," Simpson responded, although he admitted he was contemplating killing himself on that day, but not for those reasons.

Simpson, who was acquitted of double-murder charges in October 1995 but now faces a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the victims' families, appeared to lose some of the composure that has marked his testimony as Petrocelli ended with a rapid salvo of charges.

Earlier, Simpson testified he could not explain the blood found inside his Ford Bronco and at his estate or account for some of the cuts on his hand following the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
Petrocelli also attacked Simpson's alibi for the night of the murders and accused him of failing a lie detector test.

But the attorney saved his most dramatic performance for the day's finale. "You know you committed those murders ... You went there (Nicole Brown Simpson's townhouse) that night and you confronted her and you killed her. True?" Petrocelli asked.
"That's totally, absolutely incorrect," Simpson shot back.
"And Ron Goldman came upon you when you were there with Nicole and you didn't expect him," Petrocelli continued, his voice getting louder.
"Untrue," said Simpson.
"Ron Goldman got in a fight with you and you cut him and you sliced him until he died and collapsed in your arms," Petrocelli persisted.
"Untrue," Simpson said, looking drained and tired by his ordeal on the stand.
Finishing with a flourish, Petrocelli went on, "And you left him to die with his eyes wide open looking right at you. True or not?"
"That's untrue," Simpson responded wearily, and Petrocelli said he had no further questions.
During the exchange Sharon Rufo, Goldman's natural mother, and his sister, Kim, were crying. Goldman's father, Fred, and his stepmother, Patti, held hands tightly.
Attorney Michael Brewer, representing Rufo, was expected to start questioning Simpson on Tuesday.

During Monday's session, Petrocelli contended some of the unexplained injuries to Simpson's fingers and hand were caused by fingernails "ripping into your skin," suggesting it happened in the death struggle between Simpson and his alleged victims.

Simpson said he recalled seeing only one speck of blood on the little finger of his left hand just before he went to the airport for a flight to Chicago on the night of June 12, 1994, but could not remember how he sustained the injury.
He admitted he could not explain how his blood got in his Bronco, how the blood of Nicole Brown Simpson got onto a carpet in the Bronco or how blood matching his own ended up at the murder scene.
Simpson's attorneys are expected to claim that blood at the murder scene and at Simpson's estate was planted by police in a conspiracy to frame him.

Simpson said he suffered a gash to the middle finger of his left hand when he broke a drinking glass in the bathroom of his Chicago hotel room after being told of his ex-wife's death, but he could not explain other cuts and abrasions on his left hand, although he insisted they were not there when he returned from Chicago.

Simpson also denied taking and failing a lie-detector test two days after the murders. In an answer to Petrocelli, he said he went to a private polygraph expert for a demonstration of how a lie detector test worked, but as far as he was concerned it was only a demonstration.
"And you did take the test and you failed, true?" Petrocelli asked. "That's not correct," Simpson answered.
Petrocelli also attacked Simpson's alibi that he was home at the time of the murders, arguing he had changed his story about vital evidence in the case.
Simpson told the jury that around the time of the murders he was variouly chipping golf balls in the dark, taking a shower and sitting on his bed reading.

At the end of Monday's session Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki dismissed a juror and planned to announce it formally on Tuesday, sources involved in the case said. There was no immediate explanation for the dismissal, and an alternate juror was to be seated on the regular panel.
